paras: The threatened lynching of the Porter burglary suspects took place at Lawrenceville, Illinois, in February 1888, when a crowd of 'vigilants' gathered as four men accused of nearly killing a farmer and his wife were brought to the county jail. Sheriff Lee Gowens and his deputies brought the prisoners in at midnight under a strong guard, and the crowd made only a 'slight demonstration.' A week later a Lawrenceville dispatch reported that the four had been indicted and sentenced to ten years each.

On a Sunday night, D. S. Porter, described as a wealthy farmer living near Lawrenceville, answered a knock at his door and was confronted by a man with a revolver. According to a wire dispatch, Porter wrestled the man to the floor while his wife attacked a second intruder with a poker, and two more men then joined the fight. The intruders fled when neighbors were alarmed, leaving the couple 'badly and perhaps fatally injured,' he with knife wounds and she with internal injuries and burns from the poker.

On February 14, Sheriff Gowens, Constable Propes, John Milburn and Ben Fisher boarded an Ohio and Mississippi train at Lawrenceville to search for the attackers. Two miles west of Claremont, Milburn saw four men crossing a field; the conductor stopped the train, and the posse arrested the men at revolver point and jailed them at Olney. The men, said to be from St. Louis, carried four revolvers and three knives, one of which 'showed signs of blood,' and they denied any knowledge of the attack.

The prisoners were moved from Olney to Lawrenceville at midnight under a strong guard raised by the sheriff, and the entire force of deputies met the party and rushed the men into the jail. In the words of the Lawrenceville dispatch, 'the vigilants were overawed by the strength and determination' of the officers, and 'only a slight demonstration was made.' The same dispatch added that feeling against the prisoners still ran high.

A Lawrenceville dispatch dated February 16 and printed in the Big Sandy News of Louisa, Kentucky, reported that the four men had been indicted and sentenced to ten years in the penitentiary. The sentence, it said, gave 'great satisfaction' in the town. No names of the convicted men appear in the coverage.

Coverage came entirely from short telegraphic items in white papers outside Illinois. The burglary itself ran on February 15 under a Bridgeport dateline in papers including the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer, the St. Paul Daily Globe and the Fort Worth Daily Gazette, with headlines such as 'A Terrible Encounter' and 'An Illinois Farmer and His Wife Badly Beaten.' The Springfield, Ohio, Daily Republic placed it under the heading 'Burglars Seem to be Over-Running All Illinois State.'

The arrest ran as a separate Olney wire item, which the Wichita Eagle headed 'Attempted Murder' and the Beatrice Daily Express 'Arrested for Attempted Murder'; both gave the couple's name as 'Potter.' Only the Maysville Evening Bulletin, among the papers found, carried the jail episode, under the headline 'Lynchers Scared Off,' and it credited the officers without comment on the vigilants. No paper named the prisoners or stated the race of the prisoners or the crowd.

The Olney arrest wire named the couple 'Mr. and Mrs. David Potter' and said the posse was seeking 'two tramps,' while the Bridgeport wire and both Lawrenceville dispatches used the name Porter and spoke of four burglars.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of the Porter burglary suspects, Lawrenceville, Illinois
bases: A crowd the Lawrenceville dispatch called 'vigilants' made a demonstration against four prisoners accused of nearly killing a farm couple, and was deterred by the sheriff's guard (A7); the episode is a threatened lynching.

No one was killed: the prisoners reached the jail under guard and the 'vigilants' made only a slight demonstration (A7), and four days later the four were reported sentenced to prison (A12). The crowd's motive was the accusation that the men had nearly killed the Porters (A7).
The burglary and the arrest are reported by two independent wire stories (A1, A2), but the mob demonstration at the jail appears in a single Lawrenceville dispatch (A7).
